title: Same honest score, same false alarms?
hook: One risk score is equally accurate for two groups. Who gets wrongly flagged?

knows: that a calibrated score means '80% means 80%' (say-seventy-mean-it)
doesNotKnow: that when two groups have different base rates, one calibrated score with one threshold must give them different false-alarm and miss rates, so 'fair' has to pick which equality it means

misconception: If a risk score is equally accurate (calibrated) for both groups and uses one threshold, it treats both groups' innocent people the same.
objective: The learner can explain that a score calibrated in two groups with different base rates flags a larger share of the higher-base-rate group's innocent people, and that the error rates match only when the base rates match.

claims.text: With different base rates, a score that makes any mistakes cannot be both calibrated and equal on both errors (false-positive and false-negative rates) across groups (reveal: 'Otherwise no score that makes mistakes is calibrated with equal errors.', after 'at 50, base rates match').
claims.source: v2 2026-10-16 (r14 finding 3): 'Unless base rates match, no imperfect score is calibrated and equal on both errors' replaced by 'Otherwise no score that makes mistakes is calibrated with equal errors' (plain words for imperfect; the exception is a perfect score, a = 1 and b = 0 in FC pass 35's derivation); reset to unverified. | v1 record: Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2017), 'Inherent trade-offs in the fair determination of risk scores', ITCS 2017 (arXiv 1609.05807); Chouldechova (2017), 'Fair prediction with disparate impact', Big Data 5(2): 153-163, eq. 2.1: FPR = p/(1-p) * (1-PPV)/PPV * (1-FNR); toy check A: 1 * 0.25 * 0.8 = 0.2, B: 0.32/0.68 * 0.25 * 0.5 = 0.0588. About real systems; needs the fact-checker. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Rests on own derivation, not on Kleinberg-Mullainathan-Raghavan 2017 or Chouldechova 2017 (not opened, web blocked). With the lesson's sense of calibration (PPV = a and the low-group rate b equal across groups) and flagged share f: p = af + b(1-f), FNR = b(1-f)/p, FPR = (1-a)f/(1-p). FNR is strictly decreasing in f when a, b > 0 and FPR strictly increasing when a < 1, so equal errors force equal f, hence equal p, unless the score is perfect (a = 1 and b = 0). Chouldechova's identity FPR = p/(1-p)(1-PPV)/PPV(1-FNR) also follows from the definitions; toy check A 0.2, B 0.0588.

claims.text: In the toy, the slider changes who is in B, not the score: it sets how many in B reoffend (B's base rate, 23, 32, 41 or 50 of 100), the score's rule (80% of ringed, 20% of the rest reoffend) stays the same, and the number ringed follows (5, 20, 35 or 50). Reveal: 'The slider changed B's people, not the score'; slider label 'Reoffenders in B'.

recall.question: A loan-default score is calibrated for two towns: '30% risk' means 30% default in both. Town X has many more defaulters. Using one cut-off, what happens to people who would have repaid?
options: A larger share of X's repayers are refused
Both towns' repayers are refused at the same rate
A larger share of the other town's repayers are refused
recall.why: More of X's people get high scores, so more of X's repayers land above the cut-off too. With different base rates a calibrated score cannot also equalise false alarms.
